proxy_language: Old High German / Old Alemannic (with Frankish court register), reading 'Kuonrìg' as a Germanic compound of kuoni 'bold' + rîhhi 'realm/ruler' (cf. Chuonrat/Kuonrat, Kuonrîch type names)
proxy_rationale: No attested language called 'Kuonrìg' exists. The string looks like a Germanic dithematic name built on OHG kuoni 'bold, keen' (cf. Konrad, Kuno) and -rîg/-rîhhi 'ruler, realm', set in a later court period. For Atlantic Europe, the best-supported proxy for a Germanic court register is Old High German with Frankish/Carolingian-era spelling conventions; Old English or Old Saxon could also fit but OHG matches the name's own phonology (uo diphthong, k- for /k/). The link is weak: this is an inferred proxy for a fictional or obscure culture, and the final ì is not an OHG orthographic feature (circumflex or macron length marks are the scholarly convention).
phonology: OHG consonants: stops p t k b d g; affricates pf (ph), ts (z, tz), kx rare; fricatives f v s ʃ(sk>sh later) x/h (ch); nasals m n; liquids l r; glides w j. Vowels: short a e i o u; long ā ē ī ō ū (marked with circumflex or macron in normalized spelling); diphthongs ia/ie, uo, ei, ou, iu (and ea, io in Franconian). Second sound shift: t>ts/z, p>pf/ff, k>x/ch in Upper German (Alemannic/Bavarian) while Frankish varies. Final devoicing common in later texts. Stress on the root (first) syllable; unstressed syllables reduce to e (OHG full vowels in endings: -a, -o, -u, -i).
phonotactics: Syllable shape (C)(C)(C)V(V)(C)(C)(C). Initial clusters: sk-/sc-, sp-, st-, str-, scr-, kn-, gn-, hl-, hn-, hr-, hw-/wh-, sl-, sm-, sn-, sw-, pfl-, pfr-, tw-, bl-, br-, dr-, fr-, gr-, kl-, kr-, pr-, tr-, thr-/dr-. Finals: -nt, -ng, -nk, -rt, -rg, -rn, -ld, -lt, -st, -ft, -ht, -cht, -hs, -sk. Word-final voiced stops devoice in spelling in later texts (-d > -t, -g > -c/-k). Dithematic names are typically 2-4 syllables, e.g. Kuon-rât, Hil-te-brant, Wolf-ger, Adal-hard, Ger-hart; theme-final -rîg is rare in Old High German, where the usual form is -rîh, but Gothic/Old Saxon-style -rik/-rîg appears in Latinized sources (Alaricus, Theodericus, Dietrîh).
orthography: Normalized scholarly OHG: long vowels with circumflex (â ê î ô û) or macron; uo, ie, ei, ou, iu as digraphs; h for /x/ in codas and clusters (ch in manuscripts: ihh, hh), z/tz for /ts/, pf/ph for /pf/, sc/sk for /sk~ʃ/, v/f variation, w for /w/, qu for /kw/, k or c for /k/ (c in older texts, k in Upper German and normalized), th/dh in earlier texts (Isidor, Tatian) for /d/. Names are capitalized. Latinized forms add -us/-a.
morphology: Inflecting language with strong/weak nouns and adjectives, 3 genders (masc, fem, neut), 4 cases (nom, gen, dat, acc; instrumental residual), 2 numbers. Noun stems: a-stems (tag, wort), ja-stems (kuni 'kin'), i-stems (gast), u-stems, n-stems (hano), r-stems, minor. Verbs: strong (ablaut classes I-VII), weak (class I -en/-jan, II -ôn, III -ên), preterite-present. Personal names are mostly uninflected in game use; if inflected, nom. masc. a-stem has zero ending (Kuonrât), weak nouns -o/-a (Hano, Wîba), gen. sg. -es (strong) / -en (weak) / -a (fem. ô-stems -a/-o).
compounding: Compounds are head-final: modifier + head (determinative), with the head carrying gender/inflection (e.g. burg-wart 'castle-guard', hûs-herro 'house-master'). The first element is a bare stem or a stem with a linking vowel (-a-, -i-, -o- in OHG: gast-hûs, tag-a-liht-). Dithematic personal names combine two roots, theme-1 (adjective/noun: kuoni, adal 'noble', hild 'battle', wolf, ger 'spear', brant 'sword') + theme-2 (rîh 'ruler', rât 'counsel', hart 'hard', wald 'rule', mund 'protection', frid 'peace', brecht 'bright', bald 'bold'). Place names: X-burg, X-heim, X-dorf, X-aha 'water', X-berg, X-brucca. Genitive constructions: possessor in the genitive before the head (Karles sun 'Charles's son'; also analytic 'the X of Y' with the genitive after in later Middle High German, e.g. Chuonrâtes burg).
noun_phrase_order: Mostly modifier-head: article/demonstrative + adjective + noun (der guoto man); genitive modifier usually precedes the head noun in Old High German (Gotes sun), postnominal in later periods; numerals before the head. Adjectives agree in case, gender, number with strong/weak declension.

notes: The culture name 'Kuonrìg' is not itself attested Old High German. Its spelling (ì grave, final -rìg) is non-standard and probably a game-internal coinage; the proxy treats it as an OHG-style dithematic name. Scholarly normalized OHG uses circumflex/macron for long vowels, not grave accents, and prefers -rîh/-rîhhi over -rîg. No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word since the proxy is Germanic, not Goidelic; the 'Atlantic Europe' setting may justify borrowing Old Norse or Old English elements (e.g. -ric, -wald) for local flavour, but this should be flagged as a hybrid rather than attested OHG. Confidence is low because the proxy is chosen from the form of the culture's own name, not from independent evidence of its language.
